taxonomyNote: NatureServe and state agencies treat it as a full species, C. dorsalis; it was formerly a subspecies of the painted turtle (C. picta dorsalis) and some herpetologists still treat it that way, citing intergrades.
fieldMarks: Small aquatic turtle, 4-6 in, with a smooth olive-brown to nearly black carapace lacking a keel and a prominent yellow, orange or red stripe down the centre of the back.
Marginal scutes have prominent red or orange; plastron plain yellow or tan, sometimes with a faint brown central blotch.
Yellow lines on the head and chin, a yellow spot behind each eye, and red or orange lines on the neck and forelimbs; young are brighter with a slight keel.
behavior: Usually active from late March into early November; basks on logs, rocks and banks, often many on one log, and slips into water at slight disturbance.
Eats plants and animals including algae, duckweed, snails, crayfish, frogs and fish.
Often lays more than one clutch per year (4-20 eggs); hatchlings usually winter in the nest and emerge in spring.
habitat: Shallow swamps, slow streams, sloughs, oxbows, ditches, lakes and reservoirs with soft mud bottoms, aquatic vegetation and basking sites; in Missouri, wetlands within bottomland forest.
range: Central Mississippi valley to the Gulf: NatureServe lists Illinois, Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama; not recorded for Canada.

lookalikes.name: Painted turtle
lookalikes.howToTell: The painted turtle (western painted in Missouri) usually lacks the broad lengthwise stripe on the carapace; Tennessee WRA notes genetics are required to separate them with certainty.
